{{Short description|Generalization of the notion of convergence that is found in general topology}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''convergence space''', also called a '''generalized convergence''', is a set together with a relation called a {{em|convergence}} that satisfies certain properties relating elements of ''X'' with the [[Family of sets|family]] of [[Filter on a set|filters]] on ''X''.  Convergence spaces generalize the notions of [[Filters in topology|convergence]] that are found in [[point-set topology]], including [[Metric space|metric convergence]] and [[uniform convergence]].  Every [[topological space]] gives rise to a canonical convergence but there are convergences, known as {{em|non-topological convergences}}, that do not arise from any topological space.{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}} An example of convergence that is in general non-topological is [[almost everywhere]] convergence. Many [[topological properties]] have generalizations to convergence spaces.

Besides its ability to describe notions of convergence that [[Topology (structure)|topologies]] are unable to, the [[Category (mathematics)|category]] of convergence spaces has an important categorical property that the [[category of topological spaces]] lacks. 
The category of topological spaces is not an [[Exponential object|exponential category]] (or equivalently, it is not [[Cartesian closed]]) although it is contained in the exponential category of [[pseudotopological space]]s, which is itself a [[subcategory]] of the (also exponential) category of convergence spaces.<ref name="Dolecki 2009 Init. Conv. 1-51" />

== Definition and notation==
{{See also|Filters in topology|Ultrafilter}}

=== Preliminaries and notation ===

Denote the [[power set]] of a set <math>X</math> by <math>\wp(X).</math>  The {{em|upward closure}} or {{em|isotonization}} in <math>X</math>{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=27–29}} of a [[Family of sets|family of subsets]] <math>\mathcal{B} \subseteq \wp(X)</math> is defined as

:<math>\mathcal{B}^{\uparrow X} := \left\{ S \subseteq X ~:~ B \subseteq S \text{ for some } B \in \mathcal{B} \, \right\} = \bigcup_{B \in \mathcal{B}} \left\{ S ~:~ B \subseteq S \subseteq X \right\}</math>

and similarly the {{em|downward closure}} of <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is <math>\mathcal{B}^{\downarrow} := \left\{ S \subseteq B ~:~ B \in \mathcal{B} \, \right\} = \bigcup_{B \in \mathcal{B}} \wp(B).</math> 
If <math>\mathcal{B}^{\uparrow X} = \mathcal{B}</math> (respectively <math>\mathcal{B}^{\downarrow} = \mathcal{B}</math>) then <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is said to be {{em|upward closed}} (respectively {{em|downward closed}}) in <math>X.</math>

For any families <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and <math>\mathcal{F},</math> declare that 
:<math>\mathcal{C} \leq \mathcal{F}</math> if and only if for every <math>C \in \mathcal{C},</math> there exists some <math>F \in \mathcal{F}</math> such that <math>F \subseteq C</math> 
or equivalently, if <math>\mathcal{F} \subseteq \wp(X),</math> then <math>\mathcal{C} \leq \mathcal{F}</math> if and only if <math>\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{F}^{\uparrow X}.</math> The [[Binary relation|relation]] <math>\,\leq\,</math> defines a [[preorder]] on <math>\wp(\wp(X)).</math> If <math>\mathcal{F} \geq \mathcal{C},</math> which by definition means <math>\mathcal{C} \leq \mathcal{F},</math> then <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is said to be {{em|subordinate to}} <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and also {{em|finer than}} <math>\mathcal{C},</math> and <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is said to be {{em|coarser than}} <math>\mathcal{F}.</math> The relation <math>\,\geq\,</math> is called {{em|subordination}}.  Two families <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and <math>\mathcal{F}</math> are called {{em|equivalent}} ({{em|with respect to subordination}} <math>\,\geq\,</math>) if <math>\mathcal{C} \leq \mathcal{F}</math> and <math>\mathcal{F} \leq \mathcal{C}.</math>

A {{em|[[Filter on a set|filter]] on a set <math>X</math>}} is a non-empty subset <math>\mathcal{F} \subseteq \wp(X)</math> that is upward closed in <math>X,</math> closed under finite intersections, and does not have the empty set as an element (i.e. <math>\varnothing \not\in \mathcal{F}</math>).  A {{em|prefilter}} is any family of sets that is equivalent (with respect to subordination) to {{em|some}} filter or equivalently, it is any family of sets whose upward closure is a filter.  A family <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a prefilter, also called a {{em|filter base}}, if and only if <math>\varnothing \not\in \mathcal{B} \neq \varnothing</math> and for any <math>B, C \in \mathcal{B},</math> there exists some <math>A \in \mathcal{B}</math> such that <math>A \subseteq B \cap C.</math> 
A {{em|filter subbase}} is any non-empty family of sets with the [[finite intersection property]]; equivalently, it is any non-empty family <math>\mathcal{B}</math> that is contained as a subset of some filter (or prefilter), in which case the smallest (with respect to <math>\subseteq</math> or <math>\leq</math>) filter containing <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is called {{em|the filter}} ({{em|on <math>X</math>}}) {{em|generated by <math>\mathcal{B}</math>}}. 
The set of all [[Filter on a set|filters]] (respectively [[prefilter]]s, filter subbases, [[Ultrafilter on a set|ultrafilters]]) on <math>X</math> will be denoted by <math>\operatorname{Filters}(X)</math> (respectively <math>\operatorname{Prefilters}(X),</math> <math>\operatorname{FilterSubbases}(X),</math> <math>\operatorname{UltraFilters}(X)</math>). 
The {{em|principal}} or {{em|discrete}} filter on <math>X</math> at a point <math>x \in X</math> is the filter <math>\{ x \}^{\uparrow X}.</math>

=== Definition of (pre)convergence spaces ===

For any <math>\xi \subseteq X \times \wp(\wp(X)),</math> if <math>\mathcal{F} \subseteq \wp(X)</math> then define

:<math>\lim {}_\xi \mathcal{F} := \left\{ x \in X ~:~ \left( x, \mathcal{F} \right) \in \xi \right\}</math>

and if <math>x \in X</math> then define

:<math>\lim {}^{-1}_{\xi} (x) := \left\{ \mathcal{F} \subseteq \wp(X) ~:~ \left( x, \mathcal{F} \right) \in \xi \right\}</math>

so if <math>\left( x, \mathcal{F} \right) \in X \times \wp(\wp(X))</math> then <math>x \in \lim {}_{\xi} \mathcal{F}</math> if and only if <math>\left( x, \mathcal{F} \right) \in \xi.</math>  The set <math>X</math> is called the {{em|underlying set}} of <math>\xi</math> and is denoted by <math>\left| \xi \right| := X.</math>{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}}

A {{em|preconvergence}}{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}}<ref name="Dolecki 2009 Init. Conv. 1-51">{{harvnb|Dolecki|2009|pages=1–51}}</ref><ref name="Dolecki Szymon 2014 Unified 1-25">{{harvnb|Dolecki|Mynard|2014|pages=1–25}}</ref> on a non-empty set <math>X</math> is a [[binary relation]] <math>\xi \subseteq X \times \operatorname{Filters}(X)</math> with the following property:

<ol>
<li>{{em|[[Upper set|Isotone]]}}: if <math>\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{G} \in \operatorname{Filters}(X)</math> then <math>\mathcal{F} \leq \mathcal{G}</math> implies <math>\lim {}_{\xi} \mathcal{F} \subseteq \lim {}_{\xi} \mathcal{G}</math>
* In words, any limit point of <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is necessarily a limit point of any finer/subordinate family <math>\mathcal{G} \geq \mathcal{F}.</math></li>
</ol>

and if in addition it also has the following property:

<ol start=2>
<li>{{em|Centered}}: if <math>x \in X</math> then <math>x \in \lim {}_{\xi} \left( \{ x \}^{\uparrow X} \right)</math>
* In words, for every <math>x \in X,</math> the principal/discrete ultrafilter at <math>x</math> converges to <math>x.</math></li>
</ol>

then the preconvergence <math>\xi</math> is called a {{em|convergence}}{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}} on <math>X.</math>  
A {{em|generalized convergence}} or a {{em|convergence space}} (respectively a {{em|preconvergence space}}) is a pair consisting of a set <math>X</math> together with a convergence (respectively preconvergence) on <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}}

A preconvergence <math>\xi \subseteq X \times \operatorname{Filters}(X)</math> can be canonically extended to a relation on <math>X \times \operatorname{Prefilters}(X),</math> also denoted by <math>\xi,</math> by defining{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}}

:<math>\lim {}_{\xi} \mathcal{F} := \lim {}_{\xi} \left( \mathcal{F}^{\uparrow X} \right)</math>

for all <math>\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Prefilters}(X).</math> This extended preconvergence will be isotone on <math>\operatorname{Prefilters}(X),</math> meaning that if <math>\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{G} \in \operatorname{Prefilters}(X)</math> then <math>\mathcal{F} \leq \mathcal{G}</math> implies <math>\lim {}_{\xi} \mathcal{F} \subseteq \lim {}_{\xi} \mathcal{G}.</math>

== Examples ==

=== Convergence induced by a topological space ===

{{See also|Convergent filter}}

Let <math>(X, \tau)</math> be a [[topological space]] with <math>X \neq \varnothing.</math>  If <math>\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Filters}(X)</math> then <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is said to {{em|converge}} to a point <math>x \in X</math> in <math>(X, \tau),</math> written <math>\mathcal{F} \to x</math> in <math>(X, \tau),</math> if <math>\mathcal{F} \geq \mathcal{N}(x),</math> where <math>\mathcal{N}(x)</math> denotes the [[neighborhood filter]] of <math>x</math> in <math>(X, \tau).</math>  The set of all <math>x \in X</math> such that <math>\mathcal{F} \to x</math> in <math>(X, \tau)</math> is denoted by <math>\lim {}_{(X, \tau)} \mathcal{F},</math> <math>\lim {}_X \mathcal{F},</math> or simply <math>\lim \mathcal{F},</math> and elements of this set are called {{em|limit points}} of <math>\mathcal{F}</math> in <math>(X, \tau).</math>  
The ({{em|canonical}}) {{em|convergence associated with}} or {{em|induced by}} <math>(X, \tau)</math> is the convergence on <math>X,</math> denoted by <math>\xi_{\tau},</math> defined for all <math>x \in X</math> and all <math>\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Filters}(X)</math> by:
:<math>x \in \lim {}_{\xi_{\tau}} \mathcal{F}</math> if and only if <math>\mathcal{F} \to x</math> in <math>(X, \tau).</math> 
Equivalently, it is defined by <math>\lim {}_{\xi_{\tau}} \mathcal{F} := \lim {}_{(X, \tau)} \mathcal{F}</math> for all <math>\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Filters}(X).</math>

A (pre)convergence that is induced by some topology on <math>X</math> is called a {{em|topological (pre)convergence}}; otherwise, it is called a {{em|non-topological (pre)convergence}}.

=== Power ===

Let <math>(X, \tau)</math> and <math>(Z, \sigma)</math> be topological spaces and let <math>C := C\left( (X, \tau); (Z, \sigma) \right)</math> denote the set of continuous maps <math>f : (X, \tau) \to (Z, \sigma).</math>  The {{em|power with respect to <math>\tau</math> and <math>\sigma</math>}} is the coarsest topology <math>\theta</math> on <math>C</math> that makes the natural coupling <math>\left\langle x, f \right\rangle = f(x)</math> into a continuous map <math>(X, \tau) \times \left( C, \theta \right) \to (Z, \sigma).</math><ref name="Dolecki 2009 Init. Conv. 1-51" /> 
The problem of finding the power has no solution unless <math>(X, \tau)</math> is [[locally compact]]. However, if searching for a convergence instead of a topology, then there always exists a convergence that solves this problem (even without local compactness).<ref name="Dolecki 2009 Init. Conv. 1-51" /> In other words, the category of topological spaces is not an [[Exponential object|exponential category]] (i.e. or equivalently, it is not [[Cartesian closed]]) although it is contained in the exponential category of [[pseudotopologies]], which is itself a subcategory of the (also exponential) category of convergences.<ref name="Dolecki 2009 Init. Conv. 1-51" />

=== Other named examples ===

;Standard convergence on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>: The {{em|standard convergence on the real line <math>X := \mathbb{R}</math>}} is the convergence <math>\nu</math> on <math>X</math> defined for all <math>x \in X = \mathbb{R}</math> and all <math>\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Filters}(X)</math>{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}} by: 
:<math>x \in \lim {}_{\nu} \mathcal{F}</math> if and only if <math>\mathcal{F} ~\geq~ \left\{ \left( x - \frac1{n}, x + \frac1{n} \right) ~:~ n \in \mathbb{N} \right\}.</math>

;Discrete convergence: The {{em|discrete preconvergence}} <math>\iota_{X}</math> on a non-empty set <math>X</math> is defined for all <math>x \in X</math> and all <math>\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Filters}(X)</math>{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}} by: 
:<math>x \in \lim {}_{\iota_{X}} \mathcal{F}</math> if and only if <math>\mathcal{F} ~=~ \{ x \}^{\uparrow X}.</math> 
:A preconvergence <math>\xi</math> on <math>X</math> is a convergence if and only if <math>\xi \leq \iota_{X}.</math>{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}}

;Empty preconvergence: The {{em|empty preconvergence}} <math>\varnothing_{X}</math> on set non-empty <math>X</math> is defined for all <math>\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Filters}(X)</math>{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}} by: <math>\lim {}_{\varnothing_{X}} \mathcal{F} := \emptyset.</math>

:Although it is a preconvergence on <math>X,</math> it is {{em|not}} a convergence on <math>X.</math> The empty preconvergence on <math>X \neq \varnothing</math> is a non-topological preconvergence because for every topology <math>\tau</math> on <math>X,</math> the neighborhood filter at any given point <math>x \in X</math> necessarily converges to <math>x</math> in <math>(X, \tau).</math>

;Chaotic convergence: The {{em|chaotic preconvergence}} <math>o_{X}</math> on set non-empty <math>X</math> is defined for all <math>\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Filters}(X)</math>{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}} by: <math>\lim {}_{o_{X}} \mathcal{F} := X.</math> The chaotic preconvergence on <math>X</math> is equal to the canonical convergence induced by <math>X</math> when <math>X</math> is endowed with the [[indiscrete topology]].

== Properties ==

A preconvergence <math>\xi</math> on set non-empty <math>X</math> is called {{em|[[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]]}} or {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}} if, for all <math>\mathcal{F} \in \operatorname{Filters}(X)</math>, <math>\lim {}_{\xi} \mathcal{F}</math> is either a singleton set or empty.{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}} It is called {{math|''T''<sub>1</sub>}} if <math>\lim {}_{\xi} \left( \{ x \}^{\uparrow X} \right) \subseteq \{ x \}</math> for all <math>x \in X</math> and it is called {{math|''T''<sub>0</sub>}} if <math>\operatorname{lim}^{-1}{}_{\xi} (x) \neq \operatorname{lim}^{-1}{}_{\xi} (y)</math> for all distinct <math>x, y \in X.</math>{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}}  
Every {{math|''T''<sub>1</sub>}} preconvergence on a finite set is Hausdorff.{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}}  Every {{math|''T''<sub>1</sub>}} convergence on a finite set is discrete.{{sfn|Dolecki|Mynard|2016|pp=55-77}}

While the category of topological spaces is not exponential (i.e. [[Cartesian closed]]), it can be extended to an exponential category through the use of a subcategory of convergence spaces.<ref name="Dolecki 2009 Init. Conv. 1-51" />
